# Review

Scoped to the supplied prose and AgentAdapter excerpt only; no changed files, tests, or runtime evidence were provided. The design is intentionally fail-closed: exact full container ID, pinned daemon/image/config, durable launch record before start, DELETE force plus same-daemon absence plus durable receipt, and timeout/absence/PID treated as unknown. That matches the core stop-proof shape.

Blocking concerns remain before this can be admitted as a proof slice. The create to launch-record gap can leave an exact container unknown to a fresh supervisor unless there is a deterministic label/name enumeration and reconciliation path; missing record must remain unknown but must not become unreachable. The design asserts removal fences a paused old starter, but it does not state Docker API concurrency/locking assumptions for Start versus Remove, daemon restart during stop, or required journal durability primitives such as atomic rename, fsync, local-not-NFS mkdir, and single-writer CAS. Network containment is under-specified: private network namespace is not equivalent to no egress unless network mode is none or explicitly denied. The Node process holding the Docker unix socket is root-equivalent and must be treated as outside the contained trust boundary with least exposure.

judgments.summary: Mostly sound exact-ID delete plus same-daemon absence plus receipt model, and it correctly rejects absence/PID/timeout as proof, but create-record atomicity, journal durability, Start/Remove concurrency, and daemon-restart handling are not specified enough to prove no late restart or unreachable orphan.

No mounts, read-only root, drop-all caps, no-new-privileges, fixed command/image, live reauthorization, snapshot config, and explicit withholding of G15 admission are good; remaining risks are Docker socket privilege concentration, unspecified network egress, and hash/filesystem details for replay resistance.

findings.message: Launch record is written after create before start; a crash between create and durable record leaves a real container whose full ID may be unknown to a fresh supervisor. Missing record must stay unknown, but the design needs a deterministic reconciliation path using unique labels/names and inspect before any mutation, never label-only deletion.
findings.evidence: durable immutable launch record AFTER create before start; Missing/incomplete launch record cannot prove absent/stopped

findings.message: The claim that removal fences a paused old host late start depends on Docker Start versus Remove serialization and behavior across daemon restart or in-flight requests. State the exact API ordering, locking, daemon ID check after each response, and retry/unknown rules; otherwise cross-process late start is an assumption, not a proof.
findings.evidence: Stop uses DELETE exact full container ID with force=true; old start on removed full ID cannot resurrect it

findings.message: Exclusive mkdir and immutable records are only fencing evidence if the journal root is local with atomic rename, fsync, single-writer CAS/state machine, and no shared-filesystem semantics. The evidence names durable records but not the durability primitives required for receipts after crash or cancellation.
findings.evidence: exclusive mkdir permanently consumes invocation; Journal receipt may be written after main run cancelled

findings.message: Private network namespace alone may still permit bridge egress. Require explicit network mode none or an equivalent deny policy before claiming no leaked host/network capability.

The adapter-side Docker unix socket is root-equivalent host power even if the container gets no socket. Document least-privilege access to the socket, no container exposure, and authorization boundaries around the supervisor process itself.
findings.evidence: API via Node http unix socket; no mounts/volumes/socket

findings.message: Invocation replay resistance depends on using full-entropy invocation IDs, non-truncated hashes, nonce binding, and permanent consumed-state checks. The evidence says hashed filesystem key and nonce but does not fix hash width or collision handling.
findings.evidence: Invocation ID is hashed for filesystem key; config digest and nonce bound to fixed command/image

recommended_actions: Add a single-writer invocation state machine with CAS transitions: created recorded, started, stop requested, removed, receipt durable, unknown; make every transition fsynced and atomic before relying on it.

Define the orphaned-create reconciliation path: deterministic unique name/labels, list only as discovery, verify full ID plus daemon/config/namespaces/mounts/restart/nonce, then mutate exact ID or mark unknown.
Write down Docker API assumptions for concurrent Start/Remove, force DELETE semantics, inspect after delete, daemon restart, lost responses, and prohibition on name reuse; keep timeout as unknown.
Set network to none or explicit no-egress, publish the exact seccomp/AppArmor/cgroup/user-namespace profile, and state the supervisor Docker-socket threat model.
Bind invocation key with full sha256 or raw high-entropy ID, include nonce and config digest in every receipt, and explicitly withhold G15 recovery admission until these blockers are tested.

evaluation_judgments.summary: Mostly sound exact-ID delete plus same-daemon absence plus receipt model, and it correctly rejects absence/PID/timeout as proof, but create-record atomicity, journal durability, Start/Remove concurrency, and daemon-restart handling are not specified enough to prove no late restart or unreachable orphan.

No mounts, read-only root, drop-all caps, no-new-privileges, fixed command/image, live reauthorization, snapshot config, and explicit withholding of G15 admission are good; remaining risks are Docker socket privilege concentration, unspecified network egress, and hash/filesystem details for replay resistance.
